nameStory: This fungus gets its species name 'marginata' from the Latin word meaning 'bordered' or 'edged,' referring to the distinctive margins or edges of its fruiting bodies. The genus name Biscogniauxia honors French mycologist Clovis Biscogniauxia, who made important contributions to the study of wood-inhabiting fungi. Like many scientific names for fungi, there isn't a widely-used common name, so it's typically called by its scientific name.
description: Biscogniauxia marginata is a wood-inhabiting fungus that acts as a plant pathogen, causing disease in trees. It belongs to a group of fungi that typically form hard, crusty, charcoal-like fruiting bodies on the bark or wood of infected trees. These fruiting structures are usually dark colored and have a distinctive bordered appearance. The fungus is part of the natural decomposition process in forest ecosystems, though it can also attack living trees.

idTips.label: Crusty fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for hard, charcoal-like crusts growing on tree bark that feel rough and brittle when touched, often breaking off in pieces

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: The fruiting bodies are typically very dark, ranging from dark brown to black, with a matte rather than shiny surface

idTips.label: Bordered edges
idTips.description: Notice the distinct margins or borders around the edges of the fruiting structures, which may appear slightly raised or different in texture

idTips.label: Tree host association
idTips.description: Found growing directly on the bark or exposed wood of trees, often in areas where the bark has been damaged or is dying

idTips.label: Brittle texture
idTips.description: The fruiting bodies feel hard and carbonaceous, like charcoal, and may crumble or flake when scraped with a fingernail

habitat: This fungus is found in New England's deciduous and mixed forests, growing on various hardwood trees as both a pathogen of living trees and a decomposer of dead wood. Look for it in mature forest environments, woodland edges, and areas with stressed or damaged trees. It's particularly common in areas where trees have experienced environmental stress or physical damage to their bark.

seasonality.spring: Fruiting bodies may begin developing on newly stressed trees, though they're often not fully formed yet. Look for early dark patches on bark that feel slightly soft.
seasonality.summer: Active growth period when the fungus is most vigorous inside the host tree. Fruiting bodies continue developing and may become more noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Mature fruiting bodies are most easily spotted as leaves fall and reveal more bark surface. The hard, crusty structures are fully developed and most distinctive.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies persist and are often most visible with snow cover highlighting the dark structures against lighter bark. They remain hard and brittle in cold weather.

funFact: This fungus essentially mummifies parts of the tree it inhabits, creating structures so hard and carbon-rich that they can persist for years after the host tree has died and fallen, like little pieces of natural charcoal embedded in rotting logs.
confusionNotes: It can be confused with other dark, crusty fungi like tar spot diseases or sooty molds, but Biscogniauxia marginata feels much harder and more brittle than these softer, more pliable fungi. Remember: if it crumbles like charcoal rather than peeling like paint, you're likely looking at Biscogniauxia.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Biscogniauxia was established relatively recently in fungal taxonomy, with many species previously classified under different genera. This reflects the ongoing evolution of fungal classification as DNA analysis reveals new relationships between species.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative hypoxylon canker (Biscogniauxia atropunctata), this species has more prominent bordered edges on its fruiting bodies and may appear slightly less uniform in texture. While both create hard, dark crusts on trees, B. marginata's distinctive margins make it more readily identifiable than other species in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Biscogniauxia atropunctata typically forms larger, more extensive crusty patches compared to its relatives like B.
